Upon the end of that training, the active police officers continued performing their normal police -- policing duties, whereas reserve policemen were mostly employees of other companies, schools. They were teachers of defence, younger persons who, having completed their training, returned to their original workplaces, to their original jobs, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And just finally on this topic, sir, what uniforms did -- did this unit wear, this special manoeuvring unit?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Members of our manoeuvring unit wore standard flannel uniforms that were a standard issue for the reserve police. Those were former JNA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And please excuse my ignorance, but what colour were they?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Blue. Blue. Greyish, olive-drab, blue -- blue, actually. That's the colour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, if I could ask you to look at a document that's in the binder behind tab 23. It's 65 ter 791. Sir, you'll see this document is dated the 24th of April, 1992. Are you familiar with a document of this nature?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And can you please tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I have not had an occasion to see either this or similar documents. However, based on what happened, I can provide my comment upon this document. The TO weapons was stored originally in a depot which was housed in the basement of the Kljuc police station. Sometime in 1990 or thereabouts, new premises were arranged in the municipality building. They were warehouses of the TO there in the basement, and on the first floor there were TO offices, and the weapons that was -- that were stored in the police station in Kljuc were then transferred to the new premises. However, sometime in early 1992, the weapons were again moved from the depot in the municipality building which caused a reaction among the citizens, and I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] What was the reaction?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: They asked me why that was done and who had allowed that to be done. Those were weapons intended for the Kljuc TO, and it was moved to the territory of Mrkonjic. People wanted to know why. I didn't have an answer to that question. However, I remember very well that morning when those weapons were transferred from the depot in the municipality building which was under the control of the municipal organs -- or, rather, the TO staff to the territory of Mrkonjic -- or, rather, the territory of Kula where they were stored.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, the document states that an agreement had been reached with the chief of the Kljuc SJB that the weapons be taken out of the storeroom there. Were you aware of this in your role as commander at the time?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I believe that I should have been informed. However, I was not aware of that agreement, just like I did not know of many other events that I should have been informed about as commander. I only learned about many of them subsequently from my fellow citizens, from police officers that I commanded.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And it also states in the document that Green Berets were posing a threat at this time. Were you aware of Green Berets in the area in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: This settlement called Vrhpolje belongs to Sanski Most municipality, so I was not privy to information nor was I in a position to know. I was familiar with Velagici. I never saw nor did I have an opportunity to see what a member of Green Berets looked like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, it's about time for a break if this is a convenient point. We resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wonder if the document that we were talking to before the break, which is 65 ter 791, can be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P964, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, I wonder if you could turn to the document in your binder which is behind tab 21. Its 65 ter 799. Sir, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I see that the document represents a list of people who were issued with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If you could --

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: At first glance I am familiar with some of the names.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If you could turn to the last page of the document, which is page 5 in the B/C/S, and just the same page for the English as we've only had the first page and the last portion translated, and they're on the same page. You'll see a signature and a stamp there. Sir, do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: This is the signature by my former chief of public security station, Mr. Kondic. And the stamp is also of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And the title to the document is that it's a list of persons who have been issued with weapons. Did you know of this document before you were removed from the SJB Kljuc in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I was not familiar with the document. I've not seen it at all, but now I understand that stories among citizens talking about policemen issuing Serbs with weapons, that those stories were actually true.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'd ask you to look, sir, at page 4 of the B/C/S. The top half of the page. Are there any names on there that are familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I believe that in the second paragraph Grujo Stojicic, Velimir Malesevic, Petko Sukara are members of the reserve police in Sitnica, the local commune of Sitnica. In the first paragraph under number 112, I can see Pero Ljubanic's name. That was my former school colleague, and he lived in Velagici -- or, rather, in the settlement of Kopjenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And did you encounter any of these men after you were detained in -- after June 1992?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Two of these men here, Velimir Malesevic, Petko Sukara and perhaps Miro Peric, I saw when I was arrested and incarcerated in the gym at the Sitnica school. They were members of the reserve force, and they provided security for all of us prisoners in the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If I could have that admitted and marked at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we have the date of this document, and year?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: It doesn't have a date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Who's document is it? What's the provenance of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, it's a document; it's stamped and signed, signed by Vinko Kondic, who was the chief of the SJB Kljuc. It's got the SJB Kljuc stamp on it. And the Prosecution is tendering it to show that members -- the witness has said that members of the reserve police who were on this list were involved in the detention facilities where he was, and this document shows that they were on this list. It's the Prosecution's -- accepts that it's not dated, but it's -- by the very nature of the document it's submitted that it's an early 1992 document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I can see that. We can only guess.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: In my submission it will go to the weight that the Chamber puts on this document rather than it's admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What's the base of that, that it's a document from 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, but the witness's oral testimonies provide a context. Admittedly it doesn't have a date, as the Prosecution can see, but there is a context. It isn't just a document that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: He's never seen this document, or wasn't aware about the existence of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Now, that's a different question. Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's certainly what the witness has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No, Mr. Krgovic's last point that it is a document that he has not previously seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: No, but he has confirmed the signature and the date of the document. He knows Vinko Kondic; he worked with him, and he knows his signature and the stamp of the SJB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, not he, the witness; he, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] So I come back to -- Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P965, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I now want to ask you, sir, some questions about some logbooks and rosters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And I've had a discussion with my learned friends. I'm not sure of the complete outcome of our discussion, and I wonder whether I can inquire of my learned friend at this stage whether these documents or these logbooks can go in by agreement once the witness verifies them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, only if the witness knows something about the events, if he has personal knowledge about the events mentioned in the diary. Otherwise, I don't see a point of tendering this particular document through this particular witness. So let's keep to the standard and the instructions that you have provided us with regard to the witnesses and documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So, Ms. Pidwell, we will see where we go.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours have been provided with a hard copy of -- there are five -- there are five logbooks, and they are A3-size books which we have copied the relevant portions of and wish to tender the portions within the indictment period of these books. Because of the difficulties with the videolink and the nature of this evidence, we've provided hard copies for Your Honours, hopefully which will assist you in following through this course of testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, if I could ask you to look at the document which is at tab 46 of your -- I think it's your second binder. 65 ter 2890. 2890.1, because it's the excerpt of the document. Sir, if you turn to the -- if you have the first page in front of you, which is a photocopy, do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it. This is a log-book that existed in every police station. It's actually a duty roster of every policeman for every month, every date, periods from/to, and the type of policing duty that such a policeman was engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. And we see on the front cover it says it's the Kljuc duty roster from May 1992 until September 1993. When you worked at the SJB in Kljuc, did you have this kind of log-book to record the rosters of the active and reserve police?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, we had such duty rosters. Every department or detachment had such duty rosters. Every squad had to do it for each policeman, segregated by dates, days, and the types of duties that they had to perform each month.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you could turn now, please, to the next page, which should have the number 0629-3199.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, is that your name at number 1?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, my name. First and last name, number 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And we can see at the top it's headed "May 1992," and it lists 24 names and that page. Do you know --

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you know the policeman listed beneath your name?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, Dragan Stojicic, who was at the position of the deputy commander. He was the deputy of the commander of the SJB in Kljuc, that is to say, my deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And am I right in saying that along the top we have a list of numbers and they reflect the dates of the month, and then a member of -- of the SJB would insert the hours in which each police officer worked beneath the date.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, perhaps you could assist us with some of the terminology or the coding used in this book. I see the letter D used. What does that represent?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Let me give you some comments about Vejin, Marinko under number 4. He has the D designation, and then underneath are the hours and period when he worked. D stands for "Duty service," and they mostly worked in the duty service. That means that he was on duty at the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. And can we go down the list to number 17, because I see a coding there, PUV. Could you explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Under number 17, P stands for "patrol duty," beat policeman duty that a policeman perform in a settlement, in town, but at any rate, outside of the security station. If you look at number 17 and then number 21, then number 24, from the 7th or 8th of May they have designation GO, meaning "annual leave." The 7th of May was the date when I and other Muslim policemen, since we refused to sign loyalty to the Serbian authorities, were relieved of duty and sent on annual leave in order for us to change our minds. Some 15 days later, we had to again state whether we accepted to sign loyalty or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you able to explain some other codings that we see there? If we start with PUV, what does that represent?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: PUV. Let me just say that this log-book should have had a legend, but PUV stands for "check-point at Velagici." PU is "check-point," and then the next letter is the first letter of the settlement where the check-point was located.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: We also see the letters KS. For example, number 24, on the right-hand side of the page, page 3200. Now, what does that represent?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: KS is an acronym for "traffic control." You see that the policeman under number 24, on the 19th, worked on traffic control duties from 15 to 2300 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If you can turn now to another page in that document which has the number at the top 0629-3203. Do you have that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Could you read out for us the heading at the top which is handwritten.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: This shows the list of engaged reserve forces performing police duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like you now to turn further on in the document where the page number is 0629-3215. It's headed at the top "June 1992." Do you have that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Perhaps you could explain, sir, the -- where it says under number 1 -- we see the letters [sic] 24. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Under number 1 it says "Dragan Stojicic," and then it says that on the 1st of June he was engaged for 24 hours, and then all the way up until the 13th. So for 13 days he was engaged for 24 hours, which means that he was somewhere out in the field, outside of Kljuc municipality. That was the rule. Whenever a policeman was absent and was working out in the field providing security somewhere, then all 24 hours would be counted as working hours and entered in the log-book.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, are you aware of -- can you give us an example of something which would engage a police commander for 24 hours during the course of your time as a police commander? Was this a -- what I'm asking, really, was this an unusual occurrence or was this standard policing?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, while I was employed only in cases where there was an exercise held somewhere out in the field outside of Kljuc municipality or we were providing security somewhere, then 24 hours would be counted as working hours and recorded as such, but there were very few such cases. I barely remember any.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I wonder if I can admit this document at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: When you say "this document," what do you mean? 46, or everything in the binder?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: No, just this log-book, sir, the Kljuc SJB roster log-book, the particular pages that we have selected between those dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: There doesn't seem to be any objection. Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's not an objection. Just for the clarity of the transcript, I would like Ms. Pidwell to name the 65 ter number of the document which we are admitting. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be admitted as Exhibit P966.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, there's another document I would like you to look at which is similar. It's behind tab 43 in your binder. 65 ter 2888.1. Actually, it's in your first binder. Do you have the first page there, sir? And if you do, could you please advise if you're familiar with -- with this log-book.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the duty roster kept at the branch office in Gornji Ribnik. These duty rosters were normally kept by squad commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And if you turn to the next page, sir, which is headed "April 1992," and the ERN number is 0629-2975. We see some names there. Are you able to confirm that they're names of police officers who were stationed at the Ribnik substation at that time?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: From number 1 through 4 are active police officers whom I knew personally. They were my subordinates. As for the rest, from 5 onwards were members of the reserve police strength.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now could I ask you to turn to the July page. It's head "July 1992," and at the top is 0629-2985. Do you have that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have that. The squad commander is under 1. From the 1st to the 20th, he was at Manjaca. I was an eyewitness to that, because he was one of the guards at Manjaca while I was incarcerated there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'd seek to admit and mark that document at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P967.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Now can I ask you to turn to the document behind tab 44, which is 65 ter 2889.1. Do you recognise this log-book, sir?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: This is a roster of the Sanica Reserve Police Station, and I'm familiar with it. I know that it was kept in the squad.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you can turn to the next page, which is headed "April 1992," 0629-3106. Do you -- are you able to comment on the names number 1 to 6 listed there?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: From 1 to 6 are active police officers who worked in the Sanica police squad. Their commander was Milan Tomic, under number 1. Here you have him.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you turn to the next page, which is headed also "April 1992," that has the heading 0629-3108. You'll see the numbering starts again at the top. Are you able to comment on whether the names there are active or reserve police station -- policemen?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: On this page you can see members of the reserve of police force who performed duties of reserve policemen in Stanica. They were headed by Ferid Harambasic whom I knew well, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'd seek to admit and tender that document as well, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P968, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Pidwell, I would like to ask something in relation to the witness. If I take the April roster, 3106, the witness -- the witness said that that was -- 1, 2, 3 to 6 are the police officers. Are there any -- any police officers from Muslim ethnicity between them? The witness says he knows them all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, are you able to answer His Honour's question? In the April 1992 list from the active police in Sanica that you have before you, are any of the active police members there of -- what is the ethnicity of them?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Under number 3, 5, and 6 are policemen, Suad Medic, Resid Omerovic, and Adnan Temimovic. They were Muslim Bosniaks, whereas the others are Serb policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know them personally, and to this very day I speak to some of them, and we drink coffee together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sorry. If we could have that document back before the witness again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, just following on from Judge Delvoie's question, if I could refer you to June 1992, 0629-3116. Can you comment on the ethnicity of the police officers listed on that page.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: On this page you can see active and reserve policemen, and they are all Serbs. They're all Serb ethnicity. Sometime in mid-May -- or, rather, on the 7th of May these policemen, the reserve policemen from the ranks of Bosnian -- Bosnian ethnicity, refused to pledge loyalty to the Serb authorities, and they left the ranks of the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'm now going to ask you to look at another document which is behind tab 45 in your binder and is 65 ter 2893. Do you have that document in front of you, sir, or that ...

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: This is a roster in which the duty police officer in Kljuc --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What is the page number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- during --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: At divider 45, what's the page number, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sorry. This document's -- it's also a log but a different sort, and we won't be as meticulous with this one, so this one hasn't been provided to you in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Dzafic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: This is a duty log-book. Every duty police officer who was on duty usually from 8.00 onwards had to record everything that happened during his duty service and what they did. They recorded events, reports that the duty service reserved, reports by citizens, and so forth. In any case, this log-book is a record of events, and every duty officer had to enter the data upon the end of their duty service.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. During the course of -- of your duties at the SJB Kljuc, did you enter the daily events in this book or a book like this, or was that someone else's role?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: On page 1, which is 3601, this report was subsequently checked by the commander or his deputy. On the first page I recognise my initial showing that I inspected this report entered on the 28th of February, 1992. The duty police officer had recorded what was happening during the eight hours of his duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to refer you to a particular page which at the top has a heading 0629-3754. If I could draw your attention, sir, to the second half -- the bottom of the page where there's an entry for the 1st of April, 1992. You were still working at the SJB Kljuc at this time. Are you familiar with this entry?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Just give me a moment to read, and then I can answer. I don't remember, but I know that during that period I was informed about that meeting. I can't remember what the topic of the meeting was. It was a long time ago, and I have not had the opportunity to inspect the log-book again.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I see, Your Honours, that the English translation hasn't come up on your screen, which may put you at a slight disadvantage. I'm told it's in e-court. Page 23.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, we're just having some technical issues here, so if you'd just bear with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this log-book. I'm happy to go through more dates with the witness if that is required. I'm in your hands, really, as to -- he's authenticated the book. It was in use while he was there. His name appears in it, and I'm wondering how much more I need to do in order to convince you that it's appropriate to tender at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, it's not a problem, except that what does it intend to show, other than he was there and ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, the log-book has entries for the relevant dates in the indictment, the takeover of the municipality of Kljuc, the two dates of massacres that we plead, and it also has numerous entries about dispatches going to and from CSB Banja Luka to Kljuc and back again. I can take him through all of that if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P969, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: As an extension of that, Your Honours, the next -- the daily events log-book continues on. This was a period from the 28th of February, 1992, until the 31st of July, 1992. The next document starts on the 1st of August, 1992, and carries on until the 7th of October, 1992. It's the same book, but it just continues on with those dates. Now, it's accepted that this witness was not present at the SJB Kljuc at this time because he was detained, but it's a continuation of the same book, and the Prosecution would like to tender it in order to prove or to show the consistencies of the communication at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. That's 65 ter 2891.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P970.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to ask you to look at another document which is behind tab 31 in your binder. It's 65 ter 821. Sir, do you recognise the signature at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. Actually, I'm not sure. In any case, it was not signed by the SJB chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Are you aware of any circumstances when the SJB chief would not sign a document, and if so, who would sign in his place?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: In his absence he would choose either the commander of the SJB or the head of the group for crime prevention.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And are you able to advise the Court whether the -- any of the nine men listed there were with you at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: This is a list of people who were sent to Manjaca. Under 1, I know this person personally. I meet him every day. Irfan Besic. I know that he was one of those who were brought to Manjaca. I know the other names as well, but Irfan Besic is my friend and ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And, sir, are you able to confirm that these people were detained at Manjaca while you were there?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I can't confirm the exact date when they arrived. There were three buildings in Manjaca surrounded by one barbed -- barbed-wire fence. There were between 60 [as interpreted] and 80 [as interpreted] people in each of the buildings, and there were about 1.200 people from the territory of Kljuc. I know number 9 in this list. I know him personally. And I know number 2. They're still living and working in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And those persons listed at numbers 2 and 9, are you able to advise whether they were at Manjaca while you were there?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that the number of people in each building was between 600 and 800.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'd ask that document be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I query it coming in through this witness, Ms. Pidwell. He, as I understand it, recognises some of the names of the persons who were at the Manjaca camp. He didn't make the document. Is there -- is there sufficient nexus between him and this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, sir, he knows that the police chief Vinko Kondic was the police chief at Manjaca [sic]. He says he didn't -- he was able to say that he -- that wasn't his signature, which seems to go to the fact that he -- he doesn't know the signature of the -- of the police chief. It goes to -- it's a document that came from his former place of work, and it's fully accepted that he didn't write it himself, but he's able to confirm that at least two of those people were present at Manjaca with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I see why you would wish to tender the document. My only reservation is whether this is the appropriate witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P971, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one comment, Your Honours. I'm not sure the -- the transcript says line [sic] 72, 16, Ms. Pidwell: "He knows that the police chief Vinko Kondic was the police chief at Manjaca." I guess that was a mistake, yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Yes, it should read Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly what I -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, while we are -- have interrupted you, we note that the time that you've asked for, you've almost doubled it and you're not yet completed. Where --

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, initially the -- both this witness and the previous witness, we'd estimated one hour on our initial list. When they became videolink witnesses -- we weren't aware that they were going to be videolink witnesses initially. When they became videolink witnesses, we increased the time estimate and advised the Trial Chamber that they would be two hours each.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay, my mistake then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I apologise, Ms. Pidwell. Please -- so you have 20 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you to look at another document, please. It's behind tab 34 in your binder. It's 65 ter 831. I'd ask you to look at that document, sir. You see it's dated the 29th of August, 1992. Do you -- do you recognise the signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: This is the signature of Zeljko Dragic who signed for the chief, and he was head of the crime prevention department within the SJB.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we turn to -- we see that it contains a fairly extensive list of names, up to number 1.163, and is a list of prisoners from Kljuc who have been sent to Manjaca. If I can refer you, sir, to the page -- well, it might be easier to give you the number. Number 685. Page 0059-5016. Do you see your name there, sir?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: 685 is where my first and last names are, my father's name, date of birth, and "Kljuc municipality."

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'd ask that this document be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P972, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall when you were -- when you returned to the position of commander of the SJB Kljuc after the war?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. On the 1st of February, 1996. I was appointed chief of the public security station in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And during the course of your work in that role, were you involved in a number of investigations into exhumations that took place in the municipality of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: As chief of the public security station in Kljuc, I was naturally aware and involved, first of all, in discovering the locations of mass graves. Twelve mass graves were discovered in the territory of Kljuc municipality, out of which over 410 persons were exhumed and over 90 per cent of them were identified. Plus there were additionally some 120 individual graves. The locations of these mass graves were at Laniste Jedan, Laniste 2, Crvena Zemlja 1, Crvena Zemlja 2, Vrhovo 1, Vrhovo 2, Potocani, Biljani, Bunarevo, all of these locations are in the territory of Kljuc municipality. In addition to that, we participated in exhumations of two mass graves which are not located in Kljuc municipality. Those are the mass graves in Golubnjaca, Grbija [phoen] municipality and Tihotina, Bihac municipality. I'm mentioning these two mass graves because among the exhumed bodies they also found citizens from the territory of Kljuc municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd first like to ask you just a couple of questions about the exhumations that took place at Laniste 2. Firstly, can you tell the Tribunal where the exhumations took place in relation to the town of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the location of the Laniste 2 mass grave is near the main road between Kljuc and Bosanski Petrovac, from the intersection and check-point at Velagici some 3 to 4 kilometres onwards, and then to the right, turning to the right on the macadam road, in the forest at the foothills of Grmec Mountain, some 2 to 3 kilometres from the main road called Avnoj road. I was the first one to receive information from a neighbour who is a great friend of mine to this day, and he's a Serb. He gave me information on the location of this mass grave. We immediately proceeded to exhume it. We were among the first ones to do that in early 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have the court record of that exhumation, which in the witness's binder, number 39. It's 65 ter 2518, and I'd seek to tender that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P973, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you about the location of the -- the mass grave at Laniste 1. Could you please describe for the Tribunal where that is in relation to the town of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: The location of Laniste 1 mass grave is also near the main road between Kljuc and Bosanski Petrovac, from the Velagici intersection some 3 to 4 kilometres but in the opposite direction, turning to the left, opposite from Laniste 2. There was a worksite there in the forest. They started building the barracks, and some 1 to 2 kilometres on the macadam road from that worksite there was a natural cave which I'd known from before the war, and it was used as a dump for the worksite. They would throw their debris into the cave. However, after the war ended, the first information we received was that that cave or pit was the execution site. It was flattened to the ground and levelled, even though it is some 25 metres deep and the diameter is 2 and a half metres or more. After very hard work, after taking the soil out by hand, they found about 80 bodies of Kljuc municipality citizens who were killed or, rather, residents of Sanica local commune, Biljani settlement. The exhumation was conduct by the expert team headed by Mr. Masovic and other members. I don't want to go into further details.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, the 65 ter numbers 2440 and 2443 are court records and reports on the mass grave at Laniste which I'd seek to tender at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, our recollection was that understanding was that they would be marked for identification, because you sought to tender as an exhibit the previous exhumation report, and now you're making the like application with respect to the present one, but isn't that the -- isn't that premature?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It is, Your Honour. That was -- that was the understanding. I wonder, given the lateness of the hour, whether the documents that we discussed previously which relate to the exhumations can all be MFI'd at this time, and we can leave them at a -- at -- there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That would seem to me the most efficient way of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps if I just read the 65 ter numbers out to be MFI'd. 65 ter numbers 2440, 2443, 2518, 2445, 2446, and 2452.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But 2518 you just actually had admitted as P973, didn't you? So that is now MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I think -- that was my mistake, Your Honours. I was a little bit overanxious, and I think the agreement was at the beginning that we would MFI these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yeah, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 2440 will be P974 marked for identification; 65 ter number 2443 will be P975 marked for identification; 65 ter number 2445 will be Exhibit P976 marked for identification; 65 ter number 2446 will be P977 marked for identification; and 65 ter number 2452 will be P978 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes the -- the evidence in chief for the Prosecution. Thank you, Mr. Dzafic. The Judges will now address you with the requirements for you to come back tomorrow and answer any questions from the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you, Ms. Pidwell. Your testimony, sir, is not yet completed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: There's still -- your testimony is not at an end, and we are about to take the adjournment for the day. We will resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning, that is the time in The Hague, whatever the time is in Sarajevo where -- from where you're testifying. And at which time the Defence, if they wish, would have the right to cross-examine you. Having been sworn as a witness, I am to caution you that you cannot discuss your testimony with anyone. So you are -- the matter is -- the court would now adjourn until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 5th day of February, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 25
